What is health?

Health Psychology, Lecture 1

Chapter 1, Morrison & Bennett, An Introduction to Health Psychology

Put your hand up if you are healthy.

Keep it up unless one of these is true for you…

  • You slept less than six hours last night
  • You’ve had a cold, cough or headache this month
  • You wear glasses or contact lenses
  • You felt stressed or low at some point this week
  • You’ve eaten no fruit or vegetables today

So… who decided what “healthy” means?

Four mysteries to solve by the end of today

Today’s route

  1. What is health psychology? Definition, goals and scope of the course
  2. Changing perspectives on health From evil spirits to Descartes
  3. Models of health, illness and disability Biomedical, ICIDH/ICF, biopsychosocial
  4. Behaviour, death and disease What we die from, and why it matters
  1. Lay theories and definitions What people think health is; the WHO definition
  2. Culture Health beliefs across and within cultures
  3. Across the lifespan Children’s illness concepts to successful ageing
  4. Health psychology and its neighbours Where we sit among the disciplines

By the end you should understand: the biomedical and biopsychosocial models; how lifestage, culture and health status shape ideas of health; what influences which aspects of health people value; the role of health psychology; and why health is more than the absence of disease.

First, psychology

The scientific study of mental and behavioural functioning.

Describe

What is happening, and how often?

Explain

Why is it happening?

Predict

When and for whom will it happen?

Intervene

Can we change or modify it?

Empiricism: the world can be known through observation. We go beyond speculation to systematic analysis of data.

Not all mental processes are observable (is a thought a behaviour?), so we often rely on self-report, with its own problems.

From a hunch to a testable theory

A theory is a general set of assumptions about how things operate in the world. It may or may not be supported by evidence.

Vague

“I have a theory about why sports science students sit together at the back of lectures.”

Specific and testable

“…because they feel like outsiders among the large numbers of psychology majors.”

The method depends on the question: you wouldn’t study a two-year-old’s language the same way as brain activity during speech. Health psychologists often use questionnaires, interviews and psychometric assessments.

“The aggregate of the specific educational, scientific and professional contribution of the discipline of psychology to the promotion and maintenance of health, the promotion and treatment of illness and related dysfunction.”Matarazzo (1980, p. 815), an early definition of the new field

Health psychology seeks to understand the biopsychosocial factors in…

Promoting and maintaining health

Why do some people stay well? What keeps healthy habits going?

Preventing and treating illness

Screening, adherence, coping, rehabilitation.

Causes of illness

Vulnerability and risk factors: behaviour, stress, beliefs.

Improving health-care systems and policy

Consultations, services and public health decisions.

Questions health psychology asks

Click any question you would most like answered. We’ll meet all of them this course.

An applied science, built step by step

Not all research is predictive. Some simply quantifies or describes, laying the foundation for causal questions and then interventions.

Quantify

What percentage of school pupils drink under age?

Describe

What do under-age drinkers believe about alcohol’s effects?

Predict

Do primary schoolchildren’s beliefs about alcohol predict when they start drinking?

Intervene

Design and test a programme that targets those beliefs.

Health psychology integrates cognitive, developmental and social theories and applies them to health, illness and health care.

Health is global

Rome, August 2014. The Third International Conference on Global Health Challenges brings together industry, academia, health informatics and health psychologists.

  • Recording and analysing global “big data” on disease, death, lifestyle and population change
  • Inequities in these data within and between countries
  • Mobile technology for monitoring and behaviour-change “nudging”
  • Preparing for pandemics and an ageing population

UK, 2011. Health is global: an outcomes framework for global health 2011–15 calls for health equity within and between countries, action on the social determinants of health, and policy based on sound evidence, including psychological evidence.

We experience health personally, but culture, economics, government policy and even the era we live in all play a part. Health psychology is one piece of the jigsaw.

Do we all mean the same thing by “health”?

Its meaning shifts across history, cultures, social classes and even within one family, by age or gender.

Until we agree on what health means and how to measure it, we can’t answer how to protect, enhance and restore it.

Stone (1979)

The root of health is wholeness. In Anglo-Saxon, holy and healthy share a root, which may be why so many cultures link the two, e.g. medicine men who hold both roles.

An early, broad view that included mind and body

2,500 years of the mind–body question

Click through the eras. Watch the dial: does each era treat mind and body as one, or as separate?

Trephination

Holes cut in the skull to release evil spirits thought to have entered from outside and caused disease.

Divine punishment

Ancient Hebrew texts: disease as punishment from the gods.

Hippocrates

Illness from imbalance of four humours. Mind and body are one unit; humours shape temperament.

Galen

All ill health has a physical basis. Temperaments can contribute to illness, but only through physical causes. The mind plays no causal role.

Early Middle Ages

Illness as God’s punishment or evil spirits; priests heal; dissection banned; treatment by prayer and penance.

Renaissance

Individual thinking; the scientific revolution of the 1600s; explanations become organic and physiological.

Descartes

Dualism: non-material mind, material body. Interaction via the pineal gland, but how? Dissection becomes acceptable.

Cellular pathology

Anatomy and autopsy show disease lives in cells, not humours. Mechanistic view; the biomedical model.

Freud

Conversion hysteria: repressed unconscious conflict causing paralysis or loss of sensation.

Psychosomatic medicine

Alexander, Freud: personality types linked to diseases such as ulcers, asthma and migraine.

Behavioural medicine; Engel

Behavioural principles applied to prevention and rehabilitation. Engel’s biopsychosocial model (1977).

Health psychology

Matarazzo’s definition. A biopsychosocial discipline within psychology.

Beyond the split

BMJ editorial calls for medicine to move beyond the mind–body split (Bracken and Thomas).

Holistic
Dualist

Illness comes from outside the body: spirits, not organs.

Moral and spiritual causes; no mind–body distinction.

Holistic: body affects mind.

Linked, but only via the body.

Mind and body together or in parallel.

Little room for psychology.

Separate domains: theologians and physicians.

The body as a machine.

The mind can cause bodily symptoms.

Mind and body act together.

Interaction of biology, psychology and society.

Holism, built on evidence.

Monism: one stuff, seen two ways.

The earliest explanations came from outside the body

Trephination (trepanation)

Stone Age skulls show small, neat holes, attributed to making a hole to release evil spirits believed to have entered from outside and caused disease.

Divine punishment

Ancient Hebrew texts (1000–300 BC) portray disease as punishment from the gods.

Similar beliefs remain in some cultures today. Understanding them is essential to understanding how people respond to illness (Chapter 9).

Hippocrates’ four humours

Hippocrates (c. 460–377 BC): illness came from the four circulating fluids falling out of balance, due to external “pathogens”.

Why the humours still matter

One unit

Hippocrates treated mind and body as one. Bodily fluids shaped personality, and bodily factors affected the mind.

Healing = rebalancing

Bleeding, starvation, special diets and medicines. Even then, eating healthily was thought to help balance (Helman 1978).

Echoes today

“Sanguine”, “phlegmatic”, “choleric” and “melancholic” are still in our language, and balance-based health beliefs persist (you’ll meet hot/cold and yin/yang later).

Galen: the body causes the mind

  • Greek physician in Rome, c. AD 129–199
  • A physical or pathological basis for all ill health, physical or mental
  • Four humours underpin four temperaments: sanguine, choleric, phlegmatic, melancholic
  • Temperaments could contribute to specific illnesses

Example

Melancholic women were thought more likely to get breast cancer. The explanation was physical, not psychological: melancholia itself came from high black bile.

So mind and body were linked, but only because both had a physical cause. The mind played no role in aetiology (the cause of disease).

Dominant for centuries, until 18th-century organic medicine and cellular pathology failed to support the humours. Yet Galen’s personality types were still in use in the late 20th century (Marks et al. 2000).

Faith, then rebirth

Early Middle Ages (5th–6th century)

  • Illness as God’s punishment for misdeeds, or evil spirits entering the soul
  • Individuals had little control; priests could restore health by driving out demons
  • Mind and body worked together, or at least in parallel
  • Dissection prohibited, so medicine progressed slowly
  • Treatment: self-punishment, abstinence from sin, prayer, hard work

Renaissance (14th–15th century onwards)

  • Individual thinking grows; religion becomes one perspective among many
  • The scientific revolution of the early 1600s fuels study of the body
  • Explanations become increasingly organic and physiological
  • Little room left for psychological explanations

Descartes (1596–1650): the great split

Dualism: mind and body are separate entities.

Mind

Non-material: thoughts, feelings. Guarded by theologians. Not open to scientific study.

Body

Material: brain, heart, cells. A machine guarded by physicians.

Descartes allowed that the two could interact, via the pineal gland (the teardrop shape in the head of his diagram), but how was unclear.

How can a thought, with no physical properties, make a neuron fire?

Solms and Turnbull (2002)

The twist: because the soul was thought to leave at death, the Church now accepted dissection and autopsy. The 18th and 19th centuries saw huge growth in anatomy and cellular pathology: disease lived in cells, not humours.

The body as a machine

Dualists developed a mechanistic view: the body understood only through its parts (molecular, biochemical, genetic), illness through cellular and physiological processes.

Treatment became technical and diagnostic. Patients became more passive than before, when they were at least expected to pray or exorcise their demons.

This approach underpins the biomedical model.

The biomedical model

  • Health = the absence of disease
  • Every symptom has an underlying pathology
  • Medical intervention will hopefully (not inevitably) cure it
  • Causes come from outside (germs) or from involuntary internal change (cell mutations)
  • A direct causal line from pathology to symptoms to outcomes

Reductionism

Mind, body and behaviour can all be reduced to, and explained at, the level of cells, neural activity or biochemistry. Little room for subjectivity.

Credit where it’s due

Behind many successful treatments, including immunisation programmes that helped eradicate life-threatening infectious diseases. Very useful for acute and infectious disease (Larson 1999).

Where the machine metaphor breaks down

Medically unexplained symptoms

Debilitating symptoms with no identifiable pathology (Chapter 9).

Same disease, different people

People respond differently to identical pathology because of personality, cognition, social support and cultural beliefs.

Phantom limb pain

Pain in a limb that no longer exists.

The placebo effect

Dummy treatments producing reductions in pain equivalent to active drugs (Chapter 16).

Beliefs, expectations and emotions interact with bodily reactions (symptom perception, Ch 9; stress reactivity, Ch 11).

One kind of stuff, two ways of seeing it

Monism: there is one type of “stuff”, perceived objectively and subjectively. An illness may have organic causes and still produce uniquely individual responses.

BMJ editorial, Bracken and Thomas (2002): we need to “move beyond the mind–body split”. Scanning the brain objectively doesn’t mean we understand the subjective mind: the thoughts and feelings that give life meaning.

That this was published in a traditionally biomedical journal is itself evidence of a weakening Cartesian legacy.

As our understanding of the bidirectional relationship between mind and body grew, dualistic thinking lessened, and psychology played a big part.

Freud and the unconscious (1920s–30s)

  • Redefined the mind–body problem as one of consciousness
  • Patients with physical symptoms but no physical cause: paralysis, loss of sensation
  • Using hypnosis and free association, he found repressed unconscious conflicts
  • Named this conversion hysteria, e.g. hysterical paralysis (Freud and Breuer 1895)

Legacy

Stimulated research into unconscious conflict, personality and illness, which led to psychosomatic medicine.

Psychology pushed medicine to consider psychological and social factors in the aetiology, course and outcomes of illness.

Disability: from a chain to a web

ICIDH (WHO 1980)

  • Impairment: abnormality or loss in organs, tissues, structures or appearance
  • …leads to disability: restriction in functioning “as normal for a human being”
  • …leads to handicap: disadvantage in fulfilling normal social roles

Hierarchical and biomedical. Disability is placed within the individual, an inevitable result of impairment.

ICF (WHO 2001)

  • Body functions and structures, activities, and participation all influence each other
  • Environmental factors (physical, social, cultural) and personal factors (beliefs, feelings, behaviour) shape all three

Disability no longer resides in the individual. A biopsychosocial model of disability.

Cases the chain can’t explain

The Paralympian

Sensory or physical impairment, yet performs physically at a level most unimpaired people never reach.

The teenager with diabetes

Impaired pancreatic function, but with medication functions like any adolescent: no disability. May still skip school from perceived stigma, missing friendships and future job benefits: handicap without disability.

Whose problem is hearing impairment?

Is a cochlear implant a more appropriate response than those around the person learning sign language?

Cochlear implant. Tiia Monto, CC BY-SA 3.0

For some, acquiring a disability feels like the end of life, with increased depression. For others it is a challenge to live with (Chapter 14). People with similar impairment do not become equally “disabled” (Johnston and Pollard 2001).

The ICF (WHO 2001): universal, dynamic, non-linear

Built from studies including

0

live case evaluations

0

case summary evaluations

0

languages

0

countries

  • Body structure/function replaces impairment; activity limitation replaces disability; participation restriction replaces handicap
  • All three can affect each other
  • Shaped by environmental and personal factors
  • Performing at “capacity” is not solely about level of impairment
  • Disability no longer resides in the individual: it reflects physical, social and cultural environments, and personal beliefs and feelings (Quinn et al. 2013)

The biopsychosocial model

Engel (1977, 1980) emphasised the interaction between body and mind: biological processes with psychological and social influences.

Click a circle for examples.

Biological

Genes, viruses and bacteria, cell mutations, hormones, nervous and immune system function, structural damage.

The model’s power is in the overlaps: how these interact to produce the experience of illness. Click again to go back.

Psychological

Beliefs and expectations, emotions such as anxiety, personality, coping, health behaviours such as smoking and diet.

The model’s power is in the overlaps: how these interact to produce the experience of illness. Click again to go back.

Social

Social support, family, culture and religion, socio-economic status, work, health policy, the era we live in.

The model’s power is in the overlaps: how these interact to produce the experience of illness. Click again to go back.

More complex, but more complete

Who uses it?

Health psychology, allied professions such as occupational therapy, and increasingly medicine (Turner et al. 2001; Wade and Halligan 2004).

The doubt

Some pessimism about whether it is feasible, however valuable, given constraints on health-care systems (Lane 2014).

The key point

Psychological, behavioural and social factors add to and build on biomedical explanations; they don’t replace them.

This textbook (and this course) takes a biopsychosocial view of health, illness and disability, opening up interventions beyond the pathology.

Activity: one student, one migraine

A first-year student gets migraines in the run-up to exams. Click each factor to label it biological, psychological or social. Discuss with your neighbour.

The point: many factors belong in more than one circle. Skipping meals is a behaviour with biological effects and a social context.

Why did life expectancy soar?

Twentieth-century gains in the West bred faith in medicine’s power to eradicate disease, especially after antibiotics arrived in the 1940s (Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, but it took years to become available).

Add vaccination and improved sanitation, and you have part of the explanation.

But…

Much of the fall in mortality in the developed world came before the big immunisation programmes. It reflects wider social and environmental change: education, agriculture and diet, public hygiene and living standards (Chapter 2).

47 → 81

UK life expectancy at birth, 1900 to 2013

71

World average (men 68.5, women 73.5; WHO 2013)

Guess the life expectancy

Shout out a guess, then click to reveal (WHO 2013, overall years at birth; world rank).

Japan lives longest with only a small gender gap; Australia’s gap is five years. Years of war explain many figures at the bottom. In some countries, a 60th birthday isn’t typical.

What explains the gaps?

Between countries

Largely differences in lifestyle and diet, plus war, and variation in extra years expected after 60 (UN 2013).

Between genders

Perhaps partly differences in health behaviours (Chapter 3).

A warning

Rising childhood obesity could make life expectancy fall in future generations, hitting countries such as the UK and USA with high obesity and inactivity hardest.

If you asked someone in 1900 what being healthy meant, they might say:

“Avoiding infections, drinking clean water, living into my 50s or 60s.”

Death then often came from infectious disease (pneumonia, influenza, tuberculosis) sweeping through communities with no immunisation or sanitation. What kills us now?

Large geographic variation. Behavioural links (smoking, alcohol, inactivity, diet, sexual and driving behaviour) are covered in Chapter 3.

The picture in developed countries

Apart from lung cancer, cancer isn’t in the global top ten, but in Australia, the USA and Europe it is consistently top five.

29%

of deaths in England and Wales were from cancer (ONS 2014)

In 2013 cancer ranked first for men; circulatory disease for women.

Up to three-quarters

of cancer deaths are attributable, at least in part, to our behaviour (Peto and Lopez 1990).

Also…

We now live long enough to reach the ages when cancer is more common. Dementia caused 1 in 10 female and 1 in 20 male deaths in England and Wales in 2011 (ONS 2012). AIDS may cut life expectancy by up to 15 years in some African and Asian countries (WHO 2002a).

Where are we heading?

Murray and Lopez (1997) predicted, for 2020

  • Top five killers: heart disease, cerebrovascular disease including stroke, COPD, lower respiratory infections, throat and lung cancers. WHO data suggest this is proving reliable
  • Deaths from measles, malaria, perinatal and nutritional disease would decline significantly
  • Tobacco-related deaths would increase almost three-fold

Good news from the UK (ONS 2010)

Falls in age-standardised deaths over 15–20 years:

Circulatory, men

40%

“Why do all these figures matter?”

Because the leading causes of death have a behavioural component: smoking, excessive alcohol, sedentary lifestyles, poor diet and obesity.

Understanding why we behave as we do, and how behaviour can change, is core to health psychology, and a key reason the field has grown so fast.

As causes of death changed, so did ideas of health

18th century

Health as an egalitarian ideal, potentially in one’s own control. Doctors were aids to staying well, for the wealthy far more than the poor.

Mid-20th century

Health tied to fitness to work, with sickness benefit laws. Doctors declared who could adopt the “sick role” (Chapter 10).

Recent decades

Work affects illness too (occupational stress, Ch 11). Awareness of treatment harms, e.g. long-term Valium, and a boom in complementary and alternative medicine.

Post-2015 agenda

Chronic disease and an ageing population. EU target: two extra healthy life years for everyone. Healthy life expectancy and subjective well-being are key.

Quick check: know your epidemiology

Epidemiology studies patterns of disease in populations. Is each statement about incidence, prevalence or mortality? Click to reveal.

How many new cases of diabetes were diagnosed in the UK last year?
How many people are currently living with asthma?
How many women died of cancer in 2000?
How many people in a town caught flu during December?

Incidence: new cases in a defined period. Prevalence: established cases at any one time. Mortality: deaths in a population or year from a given condition.

Asking people: Bauman (1961)

People with quite serious illnesses were asked, “What does being healthy mean?”

Feeling

A general sense of well-being

Symptom orientation

The absence of symptoms of disease

Performance

What a physically fit person is able to do

~½

gave two types of response

12%

used all three

Health is multifaceted, even in one person’s head.

How healthy you are shapes what health means

Benyamini et al. (2003)

Almost 500 older people ranked what mattered to their health judgements. Top factors: physical functioning and vitality.

  • Poor/fair health: judged by recent symptoms
  • Good health: judged by positives, such as exercising and being happy
  • In healthier people, judgements were more tied to health behaviour

Krause and Jay (1994)

Older respondents referred to health problems; younger ones to health behaviour.

Health seems to be judged “good” when nothing is wrong (more common in older people) and when someone behaves protectively (more common in younger people).

Being, having, doing

Health is generally seen as equilibrium across physical, psychological, emotional and social well-being (Herzlich 1973). Bennett (2000) distinguishes:

Being

If not ill, then healthy.

Having

Health as a positive resource or reserve.

Doing

Health as fitness or function.

Bauman’s ill patients focused on being and doing; having health as a reserve was perhaps not prominent in their minds.

The Health and Lifestyles Survey

Cox, Huppert and Whichelow (1993)

0

members of the public

0

followed up seven years later

15%

couldn’t think of anyone “very healthy”

10%

couldn’t describe what feeling healthy is like

Young men saw health as a norm, so taken for granted it couldn’t be put into words.

Older women had often been unwell so long they couldn’t remember feeling well, or were expressing pessimism (Radley 1994).

Six ways people describe health

Which category did your answer from the activity fall into?

Not ill

No symptoms, no doctor visits, so I’m healthy.

Reserve

From a strong family; recovered fast from an operation.

Behaviour

Usually applied to others: they look after themselves, they exercise.

Physical fitness and vitality

More used by younger people, often about men. Men: “feeling fit”; women: “full of energy”, lively, good relationships.

Psychosocial well-being

A mental state: in harmony, feeling proud, enjoying others.

Function

Able to do what you want, when you want, unhindered by ill health (links to WHO’s participation).

These fit Herzlich’s “being” and “doing” and Bauman’s “health as not ill”, and seem fairly robust, at least in Western culture.

Health is a relative state

Subjective ratings track real things

Subjective well-being correlates with objective indicators such as blood pressure and heart rate (Steptoe et al. 2012, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing), and with wealth and education (White 2007).

…but they are made by comparison

Kaplan and Baron-Epel (2003), young and older Israelis:

  • Young people in poor health avoided comparing with peers (who seem healthy)
  • Older people in poor health did compare with peers (poorer health seems normal)
  • In optimal health, more young than old compared with their age group

People try to get the best out of their evaluations.

“A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.”World Health Organization (1947)

A positive state: well-being and full functioning. It shaped Health for All by the Year 2000 (WHO 1981) and Health for All in the 21st Century (1998): health security, global equity, longer life and access to essential care.

From definition to national targets

Disease-incidence targets

  • England: The Health of the Nation (DoH 1992); Saving Lives: Our Healthier Nation (DoH 1999)
  • Netherlands: Langer Gezond Leven, “Towards a Longer and Healthier Life” (2003)

Behavioural targets

  • Belgium: reduce smoking, fat intake and fatal accidents; increase vaccination uptake and screening in over-50s

Progress

Lower mortality in developed countries from lung, colon and prostate cancer in men and breast and colorectal cancer in women; less smoking uptake among young males.

Which definition would you choose?

WHO (1947)

Complete physical, mental and social well-being.

Critique: “complete” is unrealistic with an ageing population and chronic disease; most of us will have some symptoms as we age (Huber et al. 2011).

Bircher (2005)

“A dynamic state of well-being characterized by a physical and mental potential, which satisfies the demands of life commensurate with age, culture, and personal responsibility.”

Strength: context-aware; places the individual centrally, which WHO does not.

Health policy recognises the behaviour–health link, but often fails to address socio-economic and cultural influences (Chapter 2). The fascination: why do some people respond one way to illness or disability, and others quite differently?

“Normal” health depends on where, and when, you live

Cultures vary in health beliefs, attributions and practices, shaped by economic, political and cultural climate.

Pregnancy

Medicalised in most Western societies; naturalised in many developing regions.

Stigma

In some South Asian and Eastern European communities, a relative with a disability, dementia or depression may affect siblings’ marriage chances or the family’s social standing (Ahmad 2000; Mackenzie 2006; Moriarty et al. 2011).

Such beliefs influence whether symptoms are disclosed and help is sought (Vaughn et al. 2009; Chapter 9).

Mind, body and soul: divided or whole?

Chalmers (1996): Westerners split care of mind, body and soul between psychologists and psychiatrists, doctors, and clergy. In some African cultures the three are integrated, in how people see them and how they are cared for.

Similar holistic views appear in Eastern and Aboriginal Australian cultures (e.g. Swami et al. 2009): social and community norms and rituals, biology, spirituality and relationships all explain health.

Spiritual and supernatural beliefs

  • Spiritual well-being now appears in many quality-of-life measures (Chapter 14)
  • “Hexes” and the “evil eye” may share blame for illness; British Gujarati Indians endorsed such causes more than British Caucasians (Jobanputra and Furnham 2005)
  • Among some Hindus and Sikhs, disability and even dementia may be seen as punishment for past sins in the family (Katbamna et al. 2000; Mackenzie 2006)

These beliefs can profoundly affect living with illness, or caring for someone who is ill (Chapter 15).

Individualist or collectivist?

Individualistic

Responsibility lies with the individual; rights above duties; behaviour driven by individual needs and wants. Promotes an independent self. More typical of Western Europe.

Collectivist

The individual as part of a wider unit; duties above rights; actions motivated by interconnectedness and group membership. Promotes an interdependent self, which views health as social functioning. More typical of Eastern and African cultures.

Malawi: preventing tropical disease (Morrison et al. 1999)

Social preventive actions were followed more consistently than personal ones: clearing reed beds together, versus bathing in piped water or taking one’s own dose of chloroquine.

Compare how long the West ignored the evidence on passive smoking.

Balance, fate and external causes

Yin and yang

Chinese Singaporean adults see health as harmony between internal and external systems; imbalance compromises health (Bishop and Teng 1992; Quah and Bishop 1996).

Hot and cold

Other Asian cultures, e.g. Vietnamese, hold beliefs about balancing “hot” and “cold”. Sound familiar from the humours?

Fate and God’s will

In Eastern cultures illness is commonly attributed to predestination; African Americans and Latinos attribute illness externally more than White Americans (Vaughn et al. 2009).

Within the USA (Vandello and Cohen 1999)

Hawaii, the Deep South and New York State were more collectivist than the Midwest and North East. Collectivism was higher with more ethnic minority residents, stronger still when former slavery was included, and correlated with poverty.

Variation exists within cultures too, especially with multiple cultural influences (Tov and Diener 2007), e.g. Singapore, where Asian and Western influences affect well-being differently (Wong et al. 2011).

Using more than one medicine

  • In the West, Western medicine dominates, with growing alternative and complementary therapy
  • Malawi: a faith healer or herbalist, and a clinic for antibiotics (Ager et al. 1996)
  • Malaysia: Western medicine dominant, but traditional bomohs (faith healers) available (Swami et al. 2009)
  • Aboriginal communities: spiritual causes of illness alongside Western symptom control (Devanesen 2000); traditional healing used by some in cancer treatment (Shahid et al. 2010)

Photo: traditional Chinese medicines on sale. David Stanley, CC BY 2.0

Religion matters

In 721 Malaysian adults, Muslim participants held stronger beliefs in religion and fate as influences on recovery than Buddhist or Catholic participants, and were more likely to believe illness was uncontrollable (Swami et al. 2009).

We need more research on religion and health, across and within cultures.

How people think about health shapes their expectations, behaviour and use of health care. Health promotion must take this into account (Chapters 6 and 7).

Views change over time, too

Alcohol dependence

legal and moral problem, deviant→a disease, treated in clinics

Smoking

glamorous, desirable→undesirable, a sign of weak will(prevalence falling)

Illicit drug use

prohibition→criminalisation→an illness needing treatment

What a culture defines as normal, deviant or sick shapes how others respond (Chapter 3).

Health beliefs develop

Illness, disability and hospitalisation can happen at any age (think childhood asthma, epilepsy, diabetes). Development comes from the interaction of:

Learning

A relatively permanent change in knowledge, skill or ability as a result of experience.

Experience

What we do, see, hear, feel, think.

Maturation

Growth in thought, behaviour or body attributed to a genetically determined sequence, rather than experience.

Erikson described eight life stages (five in childhood, three in adulthood) varying in cognitive functioning, language and communication, understanding of illness, and health-care behaviour. Each matters for understanding instructions, expressing pain or seeking care. We can’t assume adult models apply to children, or to adolescents, for whom social influence is so salient (Holmbeck 2002).

Piaget’s stages of cognitive development

A maturational framework: everyone passes through the stages in sequence.

Birth–2

Sensorimotor

World understood through sensation and movement; no symbolic thought; reflexive to voluntary action.

2–7

Preoperational

Symbolic thought, simple logic, language; generally egocentric.

7–11

Concrete operational

Logic develops hugely; mental operations such as mental arithmetic.

12 to adulthood

Formal operational

Abstract thought, imagination, deductive reasoning. Not everyone reaches this level.

How do children explain illness?

Bibace and Walsh (1980) asked 3–13-year-olds about knowledge (“What is a cold?”), experience (“Were you ever sick?”), cause (“How does someone get a cold?”) and recovery. Guess the type of explanation, then click.

What this means for care

Preoperational

Health and illness are black and white opposites, not a continuum. Slow to take others’ perspectives, so not very sympathetic to an ill family member who takes attention away.

Concrete operational

Can’t separate mind and body until about 11. Medical staff have absolute authority, yet children weigh pros and cons (reluctance to give blood, “you hurt me for nothing”). Encourage some personal control and expression of fears. Parents must balance monitoring with overprotection, which can foster dependency (Chapter 15).

Adolescence

A social construct a few generations old; many societies mark the move to adulthood with a ritual. Early adolescence (11–13): peers outweigh parents and health-damaging behaviour such as smoking often starts. More sense of personal control, but may skip treatment that disrupts goals or peer approval; minimising autonomy backfires (Holmbeck et al. 2002).

Bibace and Walsh focused on causality; findings supported by Koopman et al. (2004). Children also think about controllability and severity (Forrest et al. 2006; Gray and Rutter 2007).

But are children really so limited?

Normandeau et al. (1998): 0 Canadian children aged 5–12 talked about health in terms of their own daily lives.

Being functional

Sports, absence of disease. Older: sports and physiology; younger: “going outside”. Older children rated “not being sick” as more important.

Mental health

Well-being, looking healthy, feeling good about oneself, good relationships. Older: self-concept; younger: relationships.

Lifestyle behaviour

Diet, hygiene, sleep. Older children mentioned diet more.

No gender or socio-economic effects. Even five-year-olds gave multidimensional concepts, including mental health. Perhaps asking about their own lives, not hypotheticals, explains the difference. Illness concepts may come from experience and knowledge, not fixed stages.

Adulthood and Laslett’s four “ages”

3–13

1st age

Dependency, childhood, education.

adolescence, adulthood

2nd age

Independence, maturity, responsibility. Early adulthood (17–40), middle age (40–60).

65+

3rd age

A period of fulfilment; not everyone becomes ill or infirm.

80+

4th age

The “oldest old”: disability and dependence; health declines faster.

Adults are less likely than adolescents to adopt new risk behaviours and more likely to protect their health (Chapter 4). Marriage benefited men’s health but not women’s (Macintyre 1986; Blaxter 1987), perhaps through differential social support; more women working may change this.

Middle age: doubts, reappraisal and change, the “empty nest”, greying hair, weight gain, stiff joints, sometimes prompting positive behaviour change.

What do you think? Is middle age a state of mind? Are you as young as you feel?

An ageing world

0

of the world is over 60 (8.6% in 1980)

0

people over 80 (1.7% of the world; UN 2013)

0

of the UK aged 60+ by 2058 (22% now)

0

older people projected to outnumber children

  • Over-65s worldwide: 5.2% in 1950, projected 10% by 2025
  • By 2075, older people projected to be half of all “dependants”
  • Driven by fewer births and longer life expectancy
  • Incidence of many diseases rises with age: obvious implications for health and social care
  • 85% may have a chronic condition (Woods 2008); main problems: memory loss, incontinence, depression, falls, immobility (UN 2013)

Does ageing change how we see ourselves?

Self-concept is stable

Our conscious beliefs about ourselves stay relatively stable as we age (Baltes and Baltes 1990; Coleman 1999). New challenges don’t make ageing itself a problem, despite ageism in many industrialised countries.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing: poorer enjoyment of life predicts premature death, so subjective well-being matters at any age.

But expectations can harm

  • Expecting poor health leads to fewer health checks; protective behaviour seems pointless
  • Poor mobility, feet or digestion seen as inevitable, so symptoms go unreported (Sarkisian et al. 2001)
  • Exercise declines from fear of overexertion; older people underestimate their capacity (Chapter 4)
  • Yet many keep a positive view of health despite objective illness

What is “successful ageing”?

Bowling and Iliffe (2006): 999 people over 65. Five models classified each person as successfully aged or not. Which best predicted rating quality of life as “good”?

Odds of rating QoL “good” if classed as successfully aged

Lay model
more than 5×
Broader biomedical
3.2×
Biomedical
2.6×
Psychological resources
2.4×
Social functioning
1.99×
  • Biomedical: physical and psychiatric diagnoses, functional ability
  • Broader biomedical: plus social engagement and activity
  • Social functioning: networks and social support
  • Psychological resources: optimism, self-efficacy, purpose, coping, self-worth
  • Lay: all the above plus income and perceived social capital (safety, pollution, places to walk)

A holistic model is “better”, and gives more targets for intervention. Caveat: 98% of the sample was white.

Spotlight: measuring self-rated health

“How is your health in general?”

  • Weakly related to objective health markers (Berg et al. 2006)…
  • …yet this single item predicts major outcomes, including mortality (Bond et al. 2006; Sargent-Cox et al. 2010)
  • Most adults in almost all European countries rate their health good or very good, which doesn’t mean they are objectively healthier

Self-reports bring challenges

  • Age composition of the sample matters
  • Deeg and Kriegsman (2003) found the link to outcomes only for men
  • Across the EU, men rate their health better; ratings drop after 45 and again after 65 (OECD 2012)
  • Socio-economic influences too (Chapter 2)

How you ask changes what you find

Sargent-Cox et al.: over 2,000 Australians aged 65+, assessed seven times, 1992–2004, with three versions of the question.

Global

“Rate your current health.”

Found: a steep decline over 12 years.

Age-group comparison

“Compared with others your age…”
Predicted: improves via downward comparison.

Found: became more negative (in men, except the youngest).

Temporal comparison

“Compared with your previous self…”
Predicted: worsens.

Found: more negative, then a ceiling effect: “same as last year”.

“Same as last year” could be misread as health being better than expected, when it may mean “it can’t get any worse”. The measures we use shape our results and interpretations (see Chapter 5).

Health is a continuum

Not sick versus healthy, but a range from illness to optimal wellness. Some may never experience optimal wellness. Where are you today?

IllnessOptimal wellness

“Health refers to a state of being that is largely taken for granted.”Radley (1994, p. 5). Often appreciated only when lost.

Where health psychology sits

Health psychology grew out of social psychology, behaviourism, clinical and cognitive psychology, and works alongside medicine, sociology and health economics. Each neighbour challenges mind–body dualism, but with different theory and methods. Click one.

Psychosomatic medicine

1930s. Psychoanalysts such as Alexander and Freud. Mind and body are both involved: where no organic cause is found, the mind may trigger a measurable physical response. Early claims that a personality leads to a disease (Alexander’s “ulcer-prone personality”; Freud’s hysterical paralysis) had limited evidence, but laid groundwork, e.g. hostility and heart disease (Ch 11). Until the 1960s mainly psychoanalytic: asthma, ulcers, migraine from repressed emotion. Downside: illnesses without organic cause dismissed as “psychosomatic” (psychogenic) and left untreated. Today: psychophysiological, mixed explanations; it led to behavioural medicine and health psychology.

Behavioural medicine

1970s. Interdisciplinary: psychology, sociology, health education applied to medicine (Schwartz and Weiss 1977). Uses behavioural principles (classical and operant conditioning) to test prevention and rehabilitation techniques, e.g. biofeedback (Ch 13). Prevention gets less attention than treatment and rehabilitation: a key difference from health psychology.

Behavioural health

Matarazzo distinguished it from behavioural medicine: concerned with health enhancement and disease prevention in the well, rather than those who are ill. Not a stand-alone discipline; absorbed into areas such as health psychology (Chapters 2–4).

Medical psychology

A profession more than a discipline, and varies by country. UK: now usually called health psychologists. Netherlands: psychology degree, health psychology master’s (1–2 years), 2-year internship; or clinical training with 4 more years for specialist certification (Soons and Denollet 2009). USA: a clinical psychologist incorporating physical medicine; some can prescribe.

Medical sociology

Health and illness in terms of social factors: a wider (macro) view of the individual within family, kinship and culture. Health psychology traditionally focuses more on the individual’s cognitions and responses. A more critical, reflective health psychology blurs the boundary.

Clinical psychology

Often confused with health psychology! Concerned with mental health: diagnosis and treatment of personality disorders, phobias, anxiety, depression, eating disorders. Practitioners in health care using cognitive and behavioural principles, which also inform health psychology. The difference: the populations we work with and professional status.

Health psychology

A discipline within psychology: first and foremost psychologists (unlike interdisciplinary behavioural medicine). Emerged in the late 1970s with a biopsychosocial approach (Engel). Covers aetiology, prevention and treatment of physical illness, and promotion and maintenance of health. Requires understanding of body systems: nervous, endocrine, immune, respiratory, digestive (Ch 8).

Which field am I?

Discuss with a neighbour, then click to reveal.

“I treat depression, phobias and eating disorders in a health-care setting.”
“In the 1930s I proposed an ulcer-prone personality.”
“I use biofeedback, based on operant conditioning, mainly in treatment and rehabilitation.”
“I study health in terms of family, kinship and culture, at a macro level.”
“I’m first and foremost a psychologist, using a biopsychosocial approach to prevention, illness and health promotion.”

Health psychology today

Roles differ by country

“Clinical health psychology” in the USA: a health psychologist in clinical settings. In the UK: a clinical psychologist working with physical health. In the UK, academic health psychologists research and teach; practitioners do further training, often in the NHS, e.g. pain or rehabilitation clinics.

New alignments

With public health: immunisation, epidemics, health education (McManus 2014). Critical health psychology challenges an overly individualistic focus. The title is recognised by the BPS, HCPC, and the American and Australian psychological societies.

Integration, not addition

The BPS model was once treated as three separate influences (Crossley 2000). Today research looks at their interplay. Example: women’s work stress wasn’t an issue in the 1900s; changing roles created new health issues.

Humans don’t operate in a vacuum: family, politicians, culture and era shape our thoughts and behaviour. Beware complacency; keep reflecting and critiquing, from theory through rigorous research to policy and practice (de Bruin and Johnston 2012).

Can we solve the four mysteries now?

Phantom limb pain

Reductionism can’t explain it; mind and body interact (monism).

The placebo

Beliefs and expectations interact with bodily reactions.

The Paralympian

ICF: impairment doesn’t inevitably cause disability; environment and personal factors matter.

Ill but “extremely healthy”

Lay health is being, having and doing; it is relative and self-rated, and self-ratings predict mortality.

Summary

What is health?

Having, doing and being: a reserve, absence of illness, well-being, fitness and function. Taken for granted until challenged.

How has it been viewed?

From holistic, to dualist, and back towards holism: the biomedical model challenged by the biopsychosocial.

Culture

Collectivist or individualistic orientations shape explanations for health and illness, and behaviour.

Lifespan

Children can explain health in complex, multidimensional terms; expectations change with background, experience and development.

Health psychology

The study of health, illness and health-care practices, aiming to understand, explain and predict so that effective interventions reduce the physical and emotional costs of risky behaviour and illness. Holistic, but fundamentally psychological.
